title: Internal Medicine III: Infectious Diseases
description: Clinical management of malaria, HIV and opportunistic infections, meningitis, sepsis, and tropical and emerging infections in Nigeria.

topics.title: Malaria
topics.summary: Clinical features, severe malaria criteria, diagnosis and treatment.

notes.b: Malaria in Nigeria is mostly caused by Plasmodium falciparum, transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, with year-round transmission in the south and seasonal peaks in the north. Uncomplicated malaria: fever, chills, headache, myalgia, vomiting; young children, pregnant women, people with sickle cell disease and non-immune travellers are at highest risk. Diagnosis must be parasitological before treatment: rapid diagnostic tests (HRP2-based — may stay positive for weeks after treatment; HRP2 deletions are emerging) or microscopy of thick (detection) and thin (species, parasite density) Giemsa-stained films. Severe malaria (WHO): impaired consciousness (cerebral malaria), prostration, multiple convulsions, acidosis/deep breathing, hypoglycaemia (< 2.2 mmol/L), severe anaemia (Hb < 5 g/dL in children, < 7 in adults), renal impairment, jaundice, pulmonary oedema, significant bleeding, shock, and hyperparasitaemia (> 10%).
k: HRP2 RDT stays positive for weeks
Severe criteria: coma, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, Hb < 5

notes.b: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria: artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for 3 days — artemether–lumefantrine (twice daily with fatty food) or artesunate–amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine; ACTs are now recommended in all trimesters of pregnancy. Severe malaria: IV (or IM) artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours then daily until able to take oral treatment (minimum 24 hours), followed by a full ACT course; quinine if artesunate unavailable (causes hypoglycaemia). Pre-referral rectal artesunate for young children when injections are not possible. Supportive care: check and correct glucose, treat seizures, transfuse for severe anaemia, fluids cautiously, manage AKI, and treat co-infection (bacteraemia often coexists in children). Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis may occur 1–3 weeks later. Chloroquine and SP monotherapy are no longer used for treatment due to resistance; partial artemisinin resistance (kelch13 mutations) has emerged in East Africa.

topics.title: HIV Disease and Opportunistic Infections
topics.summary: Clinical staging, advanced HIV disease package, and major opportunistic infections.

notes.b: Nigeria has about 2 million people living with HIV. WHO clinical staging (1–4): stage 4 AIDS-defining conditions include Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, extrapulmonary TB, oesophageal candidiasis, Kaposi sarcoma, HIV wasting syndrome, cerebral toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis and HIV encephalopathy. Advanced HIV disease (CD4 < 200, WHO stage 3–4, or all children < 5 years) needs a package: CD4 testing, TB screening (urine LAM, Xpert), cryptococcal antigen screening with pre-emptive fluconazole, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, TB preventive therapy, rapid ART and adherence support. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is paradoxical worsening of an infection after starting ART as immunity recovers — commonest with TB and cryptococcus. Differentiated service delivery (multi-month dispensing, community refill) improves retention.

Cryptococcal meningitis: subacute headache, fever and raised intracranial pressure; CSF CrAg; induction with single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine and fluconazole (WHO 2022), therapeutic lumbar punctures for raised pressure; delay ART by 4–6 weeks. Pneumocystis pneumonia: progressive dry cough and breathlessness, exertional desaturation, bilateral interstitial infiltrates; high-dose cotrimoxazole (plus steroids if hypoxic). Cerebral toxoplasmosis: focal neurological signs, ring-enhancing lesions on CT; treat with cotrimoxazole or pyrimethamine–sulfadiazine. Oral and oesophageal candidiasis: fluconazole. Kaposi sarcoma: violaceous skin and mucosal lesions — ART ± chemotherapy. TB remains the leading cause of death in people with HIV — test everyone with symptoms. HIV-associated malignancies, cryptosporidiosis and CMV are other concerns.
k: TB: leading cause of death in PLHIV

topics.title: Meningitis, Sepsis and Fever
topics.summary: Bacterial meningitis, the meningitis belt, sepsis recognition and approach to fever.

notes.b: Bacterial meningitis: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness, seizures; petechial/purpuric rash suggests meningococcaemia. Northern Nigeria lies in the African meningitis belt, with epidemics in the dry season (December–June) caused by Neisseria meningitidis (serogroup A virtually eliminated by MenAfriVac; serogroups C, W and X now cause outbreaks — pentavalent Men5CV vaccine introduced in 2024) and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Lumbar puncture (unless contraindicated by raised ICP signs or coagulopathy): bacterial — turbid CSF, high neutrophils, high protein, low glucose (CSF:blood < 0.4); viral — lymphocytes, normal glucose; TB — lymphocytes, high protein, very low glucose; cryptococcal — India ink/CrAg. Do not delay antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (in epidemics, single-dose ceftriaxone as per WHO protocols); dexamethasone before/with the first dose in adults with pneumococcal meningitis in high-income settings (less benefit in low-income/HIV settings). Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of meningococcal disease (ciprofloxacin single dose).
k: TB CSF: lymphocytes, very low glucose

notes.b: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection. Recognise early using qSOFA or early warning scores and act within the first hour: blood cultures, lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluids for hypotension, vasopressors, source control (drain abscesses, remove infected lines), and monitor urine output. Common sources in Nigeria: pneumonia, urinary tract, intra-abdominal (typhoid perforation), skin and soft tissue, obstetric (puerperal sepsis, septic abortion) and neonatal. Approach to acute febrile illness in Nigeria: always test for malaria, but also consider bacterial sepsis, typhoid, pneumonia, UTI, meningitis, viral haemorrhagic fevers (Lassa — with bleeding, sore throat, retrosternal pain, proteinuria; travel/contact history), dengue, HIV-related infections and TB. Negative malaria tests should prompt a search for another cause rather than repeat antimalarials. Fever of unknown origin needs systematic investigation (TB, abscess, lymphoma, HIV, endocarditis).
k: Consider Lassa with bleeding, sore throat

topics.title: Tropical and Neglected Infections
topics.summary: Tetanus, rabies, leprosy, schistosomiasis, onchocerciasis, trypanosomiasis and snakebite.

notes.b: Tetanus (Clostridium tetani toxin — tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release): trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus and painful spasms triggered by stimuli; neonatal tetanus follows unclean cord care. Treatment: human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines for spasms, magnesium, a quiet dark room, airway protection (tracheostomy) and immunisation after recovery (disease does not confer immunity). Rabies (dog bites — most human cases in Nigeria): furious (hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation) or paralytic forms; almost always fatal once symptomatic. Post-exposure prophylaxis: immediate thorough wound washing with soap and water for 15 minutes, rabies vaccine (e.g. days 0, 3, 7) and rabies immunoglobulin for category III exposures; dog vaccination prevents human rabies. Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae): hypopigmented anaesthetic skin patches, thickened peripheral nerves; paucibacillary vs multibacillary; multidrug therapy (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) for 6 or 12 months; manage reactions and prevent disability.
k: Leprosy: anaesthetic patches, thick nerves, MDT

notes.b: Schistosomiasis: S. haematobium (terminal haematuria in children — 'male menstruation' myth; bladder fibrosis, squamous cell carcinoma) and S. mansoni (periportal fibrosis, portal hypertension); praziquantel. Onchocerciasis (river blindness; Simulium blackfly near fast-flowing rivers): itchy dermatitis, nodules, visual loss; ivermectin mass distribution. Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti — hydrocoele, lymphoedema/elephantiasis; night blood films). Human African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense; tsetse fly; chronic, sleeping sickness stage — fexinidazole) persists in some foci. Leishmaniasis and loiasis (eye worm; Calabar swellings) occur. Snakebite is a major neglected problem in northern Nigeria (carpet viper — incoagulable blood and bleeding; cobras — neurotoxicity with ptosis and paralysis; puff adder — local necrosis): immobilise, avoid harmful first aid, 20-minute whole blood clotting test, and give antivenom for systemic envenoming (EchiTAb products used in Nigeria); neostigmine may help in some neurotoxic bites.

topics.title: Emerging Infections and Infection Prevention
topics.summary: Lassa, mpox, COVID-19, diphtheria, antimicrobial resistance and hospital infection control.

notes.b: Nigeria faces repeated outbreaks: Lassa fever (annual; isolation, ribavirin, IPC); mpox (re-emerged 2017; clade II; lesions progressing from macules to pustules and crusts, lymphadenopathy; PCR of lesion swabs; supportive care, isolation, vaccination of contacts in some settings); COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2; 2020 onwards; RT-PCR/antigen tests; oxygen, dexamethasone for hypoxic patients; vaccination); diphtheria (major 2022–2024 outbreak in unvaccinated children — sore throat, grey pseudomembrane, 'bull neck', myocarditis; diphtheria antitoxin, antibiotics, contact prophylaxis and vaccination); cholera; yellow fever; and cerebrospinal meningitis. The One Health approach recognises that most emerging infections are zoonotic. NCDC's incident management and the International Health Regulations (2005) govern reporting and response.

Standard precautions apply to all patients: hand hygiene (WHO five moments — before touching a patient, before clean/aseptic procedures, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings; alcohol hand rub or soap and water), appropriate PPE, respiratory hygiene, safe injection practices, sharps safety, environmental cleaning and waste management. Transmission-based precautions: contact (MRSA, C. difficile, Lassa/Ebola — plus droplet and full PPE), droplet (meningococcus, influenza, diphtheria — surgical mask within 1–2 m) and airborne (TB, measles, varicella — N95 respirator, negative-pressure or well-ventilated isolation rooms). Health workers have died from nosocomial Lassa fever in Nigeria — maintain high suspicion, triage and isolate febrile patients, and use PPE. Needlestick injuries: wash, report, assess source, and give HIV PEP within 72 hours and hepatitis B prophylaxis if needed. Healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial resistance are reduced by IPC programmes and stewardship.
